title: Roots of modern democratic values lie in Sant Ravidas Ji’s philosophy”: Arjun Ram Meghwal at Delhi University event
excerpt: NEW DELHI: The Chief Guest, Union Minister of State Arjun Ram Meghwal, stated that Prime Minister Narendra Modi is translating the vision and ideals of governance envisioned by Sant Shiromani Shri Ravidas Ji into reality. He observed that various government welfare schemes, including the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, Ayushman Bharat Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana, and Antyodaya Yojana, reflect the philosophy of Sant Ravidas Ji by addressing the basic needs of the common people. He further stated that the philosophy of Sant Ravidas Ji serves as an inspiration for the fundamental values enshrined in the Indian Constitution, particularly those relating to equality and social justice. He noted that Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar drew inspiration from the teachings of Sant Ravidas Ji while incorporating these principles into the Constitution. Drawing upon the teachings of Sant Ravidas Ji, he also emphasised that cultivating a character like sandalwood, which spreads its fragrance even when rubbed against a hard surface, symbolises the true spirit of humanity. Read More: 49.6 crore Indians move out of poverty: World Bank Data puts ‘Dead Economy’ narrative under scrutiny The Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh (ABRSM), Delhi Pradesh, organised a lecture on “Sant Shiromani Sadguru Shri Ravidas Ji” on Wednesday, 28 October 2026, at 3:30 PM in the Auditorium of Ramjas College, University of Delhi, Delhi. The programme was graced by the distinguished presence of Shri Arjun Ram Meghwal, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge), Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India, as the Chief Guest. Shri Hanuman Singh Rathore, Chairman, Board of Secondary Education, Rajasthan, Ajmer, attended as the Keynote Speaker, while Prof. Ashok Kumar Nagawat, Vice-Chancellor, Delhi Skill and Entrepreneurship University, New Delhi, presided over the programme. Other distinguished dignitaries present on the occasion included Shri Mahendra Kapoor Ji, All India Organising Secretary, Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh; Prof. Geeta Bhatt, All India General Secretary, Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh; Prof. Manoj Kumar Khanna, President, Higher Education, Delhi State, Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh; Dr. Sangamesh Ji, General Secretary, Higher Education, Delhi State, Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh; and Shri Rajesh Kumar Paliwal, President, School Education, Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh, Delhi State, along with several other distinguished guests. The programme commenced with the screening of two separate short films highlighting the Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh and the life and teachings of Sant Shiromani Sadguru Shri Ravidas Ji. On this occasion, the dignitaries on the dais released the book “Sant Shiromani Sadguru Shri Ravidas”, authored by Shri Hanuman Singh Rathore. The book offers a comprehensive account of the philosophical teachings and practical contributions of Sant Shiromani Sadguru Shri Ravidas Ji. It also explores several lesser-known aspects of his inspiring life and social contributions. Prof. Geeta Bhatt, Director, Non-Collegiate Women’s Education Board (NCWEB), and All India General Secretary, ABRSM, presented an overview of the programme. She highlighted ABRSM’s commitment to education, teachers, and society, while outlining the organisation’s functioning, activities, and expansion from its inception in 1988 to the present. Delivering the keynote address, Shri Hanuman Singh Rathore described the Vedas as the fundamental source of the Bhakti tradition. He stated, “To preserve the ancient knowledge tradition, saints conveyed their teachings to society in languages understood by the common people.” He further explained that the saints, while drawing upon ancient knowledge and values, openly and proudly acknowledged their social backgrounds and occupations. Through their teachings, they restored people’s faith in the dignity of work and rekindled the spirit of social harmony. He emphasised that Sant Ravidas Ji remains relevant even today as an embodiment of social harmony through his teachings and social contributions. He further stressed the need to establish an ideal society, as envisioned by Sant Ravidas Ji, characterised by social harmony and free from caste- and sect-based divisions. He stated that such a society would help prevent the emergence of undesirable social movements. In his presidential address, Prof. Ashok Kumar Nagawat emphasised the importance of drawing upon the philosophies of Sant Ravidas Ji and other saints, as well as the Indian knowledge tradition, to guide the development and application of Artificial Intelligence (AI). He further stated that adopting the values and teachings of Sant Ravidas Ji is essential for building a better society. The programme witnessed the participation of more than 600 principals, teachers, research scholars, and students. The programme formally concluded with a vote of thanks delivered by Prof. Manoj Kumar Khanna, President, Higher Education, Delhi Pradesh, Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh, followed by the rendition of the National Song, “Vande Mataram.”

title: Centre sets up high-level committee on 'Banking for Viksit Bharat'
excerpt: The Centre has constituted a high-level committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat to undertake a review of India's banking sector and recommend structural, institutional, regulatory and legislative reforms necessary to make it globally competitive, financially inclusive, and resilient for Viksit Bharat, 2047, according to a Finance Ministry statement issued on Friday. New Delhi, Oct 30 (IANS) The Centre has constituted a high-level committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat to undertake a review of Indiaâ€™s banking sector and recommend structural, institutional, regulatory and legislative reforms necessary to make it globally competitive, financially inclusive, and resilient for Viksit Bharat, 2047, according to a Finance Ministry statement issued on Friday. The committee will be chaired by former Central Vigilance Commissioner Suresh N. Patel and will include RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu, former Indian Bank MD and CEO Padmaja Chunduru, and former RBI Deputy Governor N S Vishwanathan as members. The Joint Secretary, Banking, in the Department of Financial Services will serve as its Member Secretary, the statement said. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman had announced the governmentâ€™s plan to set up a high-level committee for Viksit Bharat while presenting the Union Budget for 2026-27. According to the terms of reference, the committee will assess the present banking practices and prudential norms, identify global best practices, and adapt them suitably for the Indian banking system, while also providing a roadmap for creating globally competitive banks. It will review the existing regulatory and legal frameworks for banks, including Regional Rural Banks and Cooperative Banks, and suggest reforms to bring in efficiency and enable ease of doing banking for Viksit Bharat. The committee will undertake an assessment of the long-term capital requirements for banks, including Development Financial Institutions and Non-Banking Financial Companies, with recommendations on funding sources and enabling mechanisms to support credit growth. It will examine differences in the cost of capital for businesses and suggest policy options to boost private investment for sustainable growth. The committee will also prepare a roadmap for AI and digital innovation in banking institutions, while providing for safeguards against cyber risks. Further, to suggest a strategy for talent acquisition and capacity building to ensure a future-ready workforce for the banking sector. Besides, it will review the priority sector lending framework and Lead Bank Scheme to assess their relevance, effectiveness, and coordination in promoting inclusive, balanced, and data-driven credit delivery aligned with evolving economic priorities and financial inclusion goals. The committee will also make recommendations on any other matter referred to it by the government.

title: Gujarat: Industry body calls on MSMEs to move from AI awareness to adoption
excerpt: Gujarat's micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) need to move beyond awareness and begin implementing artificial intelligence (AI) and automation in their operations to remain competitive and become part of larger domestic and global supply chains, industry leaders said at the third edition of the CII Gujarat MSME Conclave 2026 in Ahmedabad on Friday. Organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) Gujarat, the conclave was held under the theme 'Future Ready MSMEs: AI, Supply Chains & Business Opportunities'.It brought together government representatives, industry leaders, technology experts and entrepreneurs to discuss AI adoption, digital transformation, quality standards and opportunities for MSMEs to expand their participation in corporate supply chains. Addressing the gathering, Varang Trivedi, Convenor of the CII Gujarat MSME Panel, said the AI revolution marked an important turning point for industry and was no longer limited to large corporations with substantial IT budgets."The CII Gujarat MSME Panel had decided to make the discussion around AI more relevant to smaller enterprises this year. Gujarat, which is among the early adopters of enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems and computerisation, is well placed to take the lead in adopting AI," he added. Shyam Kadakia, Co-Convenor of the CII Gujarat MSME Panel, said MSMEs were essential to Gujarat's industrial ecosystem and could use AI to evolve from manufacturing units into critical partners in larger value chains. He said large corporate buyers expected suppliers to maintain consistent quality, ensure timely deliveries and meet compliance requirements."The focus must now shift from awareness to adoption and from discussion to implementation," he said. Industrialist Parakramsinh Jadeja urged MSMEs to invest in research and development (R&D) and innovation, suggesting that businesses begin by allocating around 5 per cent of their top line to these areas. "Without innovation there is no sustainability," he said. He also advised entrepreneurs not to wait for external support to expand their businesses, adding that MSME status should be viewed as a registration from which an enterprise should graduate rather than as an ultimate destination."Every moment presented both risks and opportunities, and entrepreneurs needed to remain focused on the present while adapting to changing circumstances," he said.

title: Nagaland University hosts 19th All India Conference of Chinese Studies
excerpt: Kohima, October 30 (MExN): The 19th All India Conference of Chinese Studies (AICCS) was held at Nagaland University (NU) Lumami campus from October 28 to 30. Jointly organised by the Institute of Chinese Studies (ICS), New Delhi, and the NU Department of Political Science, the three-day conference, is bringing together scholars, researchers and practitioners to examine contemporary China, India-China relations and the future of China Studies in India, stated a press release. Delivering the keynote address, “Cartographies of the Cloud: New Maps, Old Dilemmas for the Global South,” Prof Nimmi Kurian argued that artificial intelligence has a material foundation in resource extraction, water use, land and physical labour. She said global AI supply chains were affecting regions such as the Naga Hills, placing North-East India within wider debates on technology, development and environmental justice.ICS Director Prof Alka Acharya said the partnership would help expand research on China and East Asia across the North-East. Lt Col Amardeep Singh Multani, representing the Ministry of External Affairs, said diplomacy must continue even amid strategic competition.NU Chancellor Dr Samudra Gupta Kashyap stressed the need to integrate China Studies into local academic discourse, given the region’s shared boundary and strategic location. The inaugural session was chaired by Prof John Sema. Prof Dasarathi Bhuiyan delivered the welcome address, and Dr Deepak Kumar Bhaskar proposed the vote of thanks. Special panel on discoursesAt the Special Panel I, “Current Discourses in Chinese Studies,” chaired by Prof Sabaree Mitra of Jawaharlal Nehru University, speakers examined the institutional, linguistic and epistemic challenges facing the field in India. Samuel Sangtam, a research scholar at NU, said India’s ability to produce independent knowledge on China was constrained by language barriers, weak research infrastructure, geopolitical pressures and dependence on policy-driven agendas. He called for “epistemic sovereignty” through native theoretical frameworks, supported by Mandarin training, doctoral fellowships and stronger academic publishing. Nishit Kumar of Chanakya University, Bengaluru, traced the evolution of China Studies in India from a focus on civilisation, language and Buddhism (1928-1962) to security-centred research after 1962, economic engagement after 1991, and an emphasis on technology, security and supply chains since 2017. He recommended a national consortium of universities and research bodies, dedicated faculty positions, better archival access and the use of AI for translation support, while stressing that human expertise remained irreplaceable. Prashant Kaushik of the Central University of Gujarat, examining Chinese language education through the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, said the field needed stronger institutional integration, systematic research methods and deeper archival investigation rather than merely new institutions. Shanky Chandra of Doon University pointed to the absence of a clear national policy for Chinese language teaching and warned that uneven NEP implementation could widen inequalities between metropolitan and regional institutions. Snehal Ajit Ulman of Sikkim University noted an acute shortage of Chinese language programmes and qualified faculty in the North-East despite its strategic location. She advocated dedicated courses, faculty development, sustained funding and multidisciplinary training to make the region a hub for China Studies. In the closing discussion, Prof Mitra said that despite AI’s growing influence, soft skills and human scholarship could not be replaced. Panel on political economyThematic Panel I, “China’s Political Economy: Environment, Energy and Regional Development,” chaired by Prof Akhil Ranjan Dutta of Gauhati University, looked at China’s energy transition, digital governance, borderland development and the environmental costs of technological expansion. Prachi Aggarwal of the University of Delhi said China’s energy strategy under Xi Jinping involved a gradual rather than immediate shift away from fossil fuels, with coal remaining central due to local government and industrial dependence. Electric vehicles, batteries and solar panels, she said, were emerging as key sectors. Saumya Soni of JNU presented research on Zhejiang Province’s shift from the market-driven “Wenzhou Model” to technology-led digital governance, exemplified by Hangzhou’s “City Brain” initiative. She said AI and big data improved public services but did not replace local institutions, community networks and human verification, and flagged concerns over surveillance, data privacy and performance-driven governance. Mallika Bora of the University of Delhi, applying Samir Amin’s framework of unequal development, argued that tourism, poverty-alleviation programmes and global market expansion could commodify the ethnic textile and handicraft industries of Yunnan while reinforcing class, ethnic and gender hierarchies. Market visibility, she cautioned, should not be mistaken for structural emancipation. Ana Sinha of FORE School of Management examined water stress, carbon-transition risk and governance gaps in India-China semiconductor and AI infrastructure investment. Identifying Dholera and Jewar in India, and Tianjin, Xi’an and the Yangtze Delta in China, as high-risk zones, she argued that technological sovereignty was impossible without environmental sustainability and responsible water management. Panel on state and societyThematic Panel II, “State, Society and Governance in Contemporary China,” was chaired by Prof Sreemati Chakrabarti, Chairperson of ICS. She said China’s recent development must be understood in relation to the reforms of the 1970s and 1980s, which brought rapid growth, new economic zones and a rising middle class, alongside regional disparities and social tensions. Prabir Kumar Talukdar of the University of Delhi, speaking on Tang Ping (“lying flat”), said the withdrawal of many Chinese youth from intense competition reflected declining trust in fairness and upward mobility rather than laziness. He said the state had responded through censorship and moral framing. Bidisha Seth of Visva-Bharati University analysed the contradictions between China’s official state feminism and its restrictions on autonomous feminist activism. Referring to the 2025 Global Leaders’ Meeting on Women, she argued that genuine gender equality required independent agency, decision-making authority and the freedom to organise. Rityusha Mani Tiwary and Saima Iqbal of Shaheed Bhagat Singh College presented a comparative study of women’s movements in China and India, contrasting China’s state-led feminism with India’s more open but fragmented democratic and market environment. The panel concluded that development models must be re-evaluated to centre young people’s lived realities and foster independent feminist spaces.

excerpt: Air India has received DGCA approval to operate a flying academy at Belora Airport in Amravati, Maharashtra, with a fleet of 34 aircraft, including 31 single-engine and three twin-engine planes. Spread across 10 acres, the facility will be India's first flying academy established by an Indian airline and will complement the carrier's larger training centre in Gurugram.
